whyItExists.problem: You finished your feature branch. The work needs to come back into main so it can be deployed.
whyItExists.solution: git merge combines two branches. It takes the commits from one branch and integrates them into another, creating a merged history.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When you want to integrate a feature branch into main. Also happens automatically during git pull.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When you want a linear history (prefer rebase). When you're collaborating on a team, merging via a Pull Request on GitHub is the standard — it documents the review.

explainModes.beginner: Merging is how you combine branches. You switch to main, then tell Git to bring in the commits from your feature branch. Git does the work of combining the two histories.
explainModes.simple: git switch main → git merge feature/login. If the branches didn't diverge (only feature branch has new commits), Git does a fast-forward: it just moves the main pointer forward. If both branches have new commits, Git creates a merge commit that has two parents.
explainModes.standard: Two merge types: Fast-forward (main has no new commits since the branch was created — Git moves the pointer, no merge commit created). Three-way merge (both branches have commits — Git finds the common ancestor, combines changes, creates a merge commit). Use --no-ff to always create a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible.
explainModes.technical: A merge commit has two (or more) parent pointers. The merge base is found with git merge-base. Git uses a three-way diff between: common ancestor, ours (current branch HEAD), theirs (branch being merged). Conflicts occur when both sides changed the same lines. git merge --squash combines all commits into one before merging — useful for clean history.
explainModes.deepDive: Git supports octopus merges (merging more than 2 branches at once) — used by the Linux kernel. Recursive merge strategy (default) handles criss-cross merges. ort strategy (default since Git 2.34) is faster. Subtree merge lets you merge a repo as a subdirectory. Merge drivers in .gitattributes can automate conflict resolution for specific file types.

content.text: When main hasn't changed since you branched, Git simply moves the pointer forward. No merge commit is created.

content.code:
# Situation: main has no new commits since feature branched
# main:    A---B
# feature:      C---D

git switch main
git merge feature/dark-mode
# → Fast-forward
# → main pointer moves to D

# Result:
# main:    A---B---C---D  (same as feature)

content.text: When both branches have diverged (both have new commits), Git creates a merge commit that has two parents.

content.code:
# Situation: both branches have new commits
# main:    A---B---E
# feature:  \---C---D

git switch main
git merge feature/dark-mode
# → Merge made by the 'ort' strategy
# → Creates merge commit M

# Result:
# main:    A---B---E---M  (M has parents E and D)
#           \---C---D--/

# Merge a branch
git merge feature/login

# Always create a merge commit (even if fast-forward is possible)
git merge --no-ff feature/login

# Squash all commits into one (then you commit manually)
git merge --squash feature/login
git commit -m "Add login feature"

# Abort a merge in progress (if you change your mind)
git merge --abort

# After resolving conflicts, complete the merge
git add .
git merge --continue

questions.question: When does a fast-forward merge happen?
options: When the target branch (main) has no new commits since the feature branch was created
When both branches have the same number of commits
questions.explanation: A fast-forward merge happens when main (the branch you're merging into) hasn't diverged — it has no new commits since the feature branch was created. Git just moves the pointer forward.

faq.q: Should I use merge or rebase?
faq.a: Use merge for integrating feature branches into main — it preserves the full history. Use rebase to update a feature branch with the latest main (keeping a linear history). Never rebase shared branches.

faq.q: What is --no-ff and when do I need it?
faq.a: --no-ff (no fast-forward) forces Git to always create a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible. This preserves the branch history so you can see that a feature branch existed. Many teams require this for main.

examples: GitHub's 'Merge pull request' button does a --no-ff merge by default
git pull is git fetch + git merge (or rebase if configured)
Hotfix workflow: branch from main, fix, merge back to main AND develop
